aboutText: An unofficial illustrated project, grounded in pinned source code and the official Q&A. Diagrams support understanding; production configuration and measurement remain separate.
modelNote: This is a conservative code guide. The official model card confirms component names; the runtime descriptions below remain explicitly marked as code inferences.
modelSource: Official DeepSeek model card and technical report

blocks.title: Why separate the stages
blocks.text: A long prompt and a reply that has just started compete for the same device, but ask for different work. In [[prefill-decode|prefill and decode]], a long prompt exposes many known positions at once, whereas small-batch generation is often limited by [[bandwidth]]. [[pd-separation|Disaggregation]] allows the service to size input processing and generation separately and reduces interference from long prompts. Separation also creates a state-transfer boundary. Its benefit depends on both the compute saved and the queueing and communication introduced.

blocks.title: How DeepInfer applies the separation
blocks.text: The DeepInfer Q&A separates the vision encoder, prefill, decode and cache storage. Image encoding supplies [[embedding|embeddings]] for later computation. A separate vision pool can scale independently of text-only traffic. The Q&A recommends EP2–8 / DP2–8 for prefill and EP64–128 / DP64–128 for decode, keeping prefill groups small when memory permits and widening expert parallelism for decode when hardware permits. These ranges are deployment recommendations from the Q&A. A general compute-versus-bandwidth explanation alone cannot derive those particular numbers.

blocks.title: Scenario: a follow-up about an image
blocks.text: A user uploads an image, asks for a description and then asks about one detail. Image representations, the existing prefix and the new question are different inputs. A compatible [[prefix-cache]] can reuse prior state, leaving only new work to compute; a newly added image still needs its own encoding. Prepared state then reaches the generation stage and the response returns incrementally. This scenario separates two questions: which old computation can be reused, and which resource should process the remaining work? It does not require every request to traverse every stage identically.

blocks.title: Content and state
blocks.text: Content and state arrive at prefill by different paths. A new image first becomes an embedding, while a repeated conversation prefix may already have reusable KV. Trace a first question through the image and input-computation path. Then trace a follow-up through the cache path as well. This exercise gives the shared-storage box a concrete role: it supplies state associated with earlier computation, which can join the input work that the current request still needs to perform.

blocks.title: Allocate each pool
blocks.text: Prefill processes remaining input; decode serves requests that are already generating. Separate pools let the system allocate resources by stage. The expert-parallel recommendations in the Q&A also differ by stage, reflecting the different work being handled. At each boundary, ask what the previous pool produces and what the next pool consumes. This way of reading turns a deployment drawing into a sequence of explicit handoffs, with the cache and vision paths joining the main language-model path at the points where their data is needed.

blocks.title: How reuse affects routing
blocks.text: Shared storage makes prefix reuse available beyond the original compute host. A prefill instance can retrieve the required Block KV and continue processing input. This connects routing decisions with both compute load and the availability of reusable state. It also separates scaling storage from scaling computation. The storage box therefore represents a capability assembled from locating state, retrieving it, and making it available to the engine. Follow those operations separately when the storage chapter expands this part of the overview.

blocks.title: From generation to the client
blocks.text: At decode, the initial input work gives way to a repeated generation cycle. Each generated token still has to pass through protocol parsing before it becomes text or an event for the client. The request therefore includes both device-to-device handoffs and transformations between application representations and model representations. The next chapter places the repeating compute cycle on a timeline. Later chapters zoom in on expert placement, cache recovery, and the protocol path that returns a usable answer to the caller.

blocks.title: Why the GPU waits for the CPU
blocks.text: The GPU performs computation while the CPU prepares requests, submits work and processes results. A [[kernel-launch]] submits an operation rather than waiting for its completion. A [[cuda-stream]] orders the device work. Small decode batches often have short compute steps, making repeated submission and post-processing gaps more visible. Distinguishing submission, execution and completion is essential: calling a function earlier does not mean its result becomes available earlier. The useful opportunity is to perform independent host work while already submitted device work is running.

blocks.title: Move waiting out of the critical path
blocks.text: DeepInfer staggers batches: the GPU runs the current batch while the CPU prepares later work and handles older completed results. This changes scheduling without removing the dependency of sampling on forward computation. With [[continuous-batching]], requests may enter and leave between iterations. Scheduling ahead therefore also requires preserving the correspondence between request identities and previous device outputs. Overlap and correct mapping are complementary: the first reduces exposed waiting, while the second ensures that reuse belongs to the right request.

blocks.title: Scenario: one request leaves and another joins
blocks.text: Suppose a batch contains requests A and B, then B finishes and C joins. A can continue from its own previous result; C has no previous result. Reusing the second old row as the second new row would incorrectly attach B’s state to C. The snippet checks sequence identities before reusing row positions. The timeline shows an illustrative steady state, not a guarantee of uninterrupted device activity. When host work becomes the limiting stage, overlap cannot manufacture missing inputs. This is why a remap is necessary even when the visible timeline looks simple.

blocks.title: Keep sequence identity
blocks.text: Batch membership changes as requests finish, arrive, or continue. A sequence that occupied one tensor row can occupy a different row in the next prepared batch. Remapping uses sequence identity to connect those rows so that an existing result reaches the correct continuing request. Pick a continuing sequence and follow its identity across batches before following its data. That small exercise explains the bookkeeping underneath the clean timeline and connects the high-level overlap to the implementation that maintains request-to-row correspondence.

blocks.title: The limits of overlap
blocks.text: The amount of waiting that can be hidden depends on the available device interval. If CPU work takes longer, the GPU will still wait for the next prepared batch. Check the length of both lanes when interpreting the idle share. The example describes a steady teaching schedule; a real pipeline also starts, drains, and changes its membership over time. Carry the dependency-based reading method into an execution trace: first identify when a result becomes available, then look for independent work that can occupy the same interval. Consider a request that continues while another request finishes. On the CPU lane, the next batch is prepared with its updated membership. On the GPU lane, earlier work still refers to the batch for which it was submitted. The continuing request needs a connection between those two arrangements. Sequence remapping supplies that connection, allowing the result produced for its old position to reach its new position. Follow this request through preparation, execution, and result handling in that order. The timeline then describes a changing collection of requests whose identities remain traceable across the overlapping work, rather than a permanently fixed matrix of rows.

blocks.title: Why some experts become busy
blocks.text: [[moe|MoE]] uses [[expert-routing]] to choose experts from token representations, rather than choosing whichever device is idle. Even with [[ep]], a batch may concentrate on a few experts. Dispatch and combine use [[all-to-all]] communication and must obtain the required results; slow devices can extend the iteration. A large number of experts therefore does not imply equal device workloads. Routing answers which computation the model needs, while placement answers where that computation runs. Load balancing works on the latter without inventing different expert weights.

blocks.title: Logical experts and physical locations
blocks.text: DeepInfer assigns [[expert-replica|physical replicas]] to busy logical experts and rearranges placement from recent token statistics. Multiple locations can execute the same logical expert weights. This differs from a [[shared-expert]], which is a role in the model architecture rather than a deployment copy. The location mapping and the actual weight movement must agree. Updating only the mapping would point execution at the wrong contents. Conversely, moving weights without updating dispatch information would leave tokens headed for outdated locations.

blocks.title: Scenario: similar prompts arrive together
blocks.text: Imagine a batch of similar prompts repeatedly selecting the same expert. With a single physical instance, its device accumulates more work. Additional replicas let several locations process that expert’s inputs. E3′ in the drawing is a copy of E3, not a newly trained expert. The before-and-after illustration keeps total work fixed and shows its redistribution with load bars. Actual placement uses a statistical window and does not guarantee equal load in every individual iteration. A changed workload can make yesterday’s useful placement less suitable today.

blocks.title: Observe and rebalance
blocks.text: Observation, placement, and movement happen in sequence. The statistics window determines which recent loads inform the decision. The rebalance interval determines when placement is reconsidered. Redundant capacity provides room for additional physical copies. Prefill and decode have separately listed official settings, so compare the columns with their roles in mind. Each parameter changes a different part of the process: the history being observed, the opportunity to adjust, or the physical capacity available to the resulting arrangement.

blocks.title: Move weights with mappings
blocks.text: The policy produces logical-to-physical and physical-to-logical mappings. Weight shuffle then moves the corresponding expert data to the selected locations. A newly arranged grid only becomes executable once those weights are present. When reading the implementation, locate the mapping output, then locate the movement path that consumes it. Finally return to the drawing and assign each copy to its resulting device. This provides a concrete route from a policy decision to the data placement used during model execution.

blocks.title: From placement to balance
blocks.text: The reported moe_lb metric relates the busiest rank to the average rank load. Imagine keeping the total routed work fixed while redistributing copies of a popular expert: can work previously concentrated on a busy device be shared across other placements? Use that question to connect placement changes with the balance being observed. The official configurations and measurements remain beside the diagram for comparison. Read them with their associated stage and workload context while tracing how a change in placement can affect the distribution of work. A useful source-reading exercise is to choose a logical expert, inspect the mapping entries that name its physical copies, and then follow the shuffle operation that prepares their weights. Return to the grid after each step. This links the abstract policy output to the device locations that execute the expert.

blocks.title: Which history must remain available
blocks.text: With long context, storing and recomputing state across all layers becomes expensive. Start with [[swa]], where a query directly reads a local window and local state can be bounded. Then consider [[yoco]], where later layers reuse global KV generated earlier. These reduce different dimensions of work. YOCO’s self-decoder and cross-decoder are both causal layer groups. Their names should not be interpreted as the input encoder and output decoder of a translation model. The entire system still generates autoregressively.

blocks.title: Then follow DeepInfer’s CED
blocks.text: This site uses the Q&A’s names for [[ced|CED]] layer groups. The encoder processes input; decoder global KV is projected from a boundary [[hidden-state]], while local SWA state has a separate preparation path. Distinguish [[block-kv|global Block KV]] from window state before considering replay. Decoder replay prepares the prompt tail on every prefill. Encoder replay instead restores state around a matched-prefix boundary when its SWA state is missing. Their triggers and starting points differ, even though both involve bounded local work.

blocks.title: Scenario: the prefix survives but window state does not
blocks.text: When continuing a long conversation, the service may retain global prefix KV but no matching encoder SWA state. It can keep that global hit and restore a bounded region before the matched boundary, rather than discarding all prior computation. Separately, the decoder still prepares its own SWA state at the current prompt tail. The interactive cache-hit switch changes only the encoder recovery path. It is not a control for turning decoder replay on or off. Keeping the two boundaries distinct makes the cache diagram much easier to interpret.

blocks.title: Where decoder Block KV comes from
blocks.text: After encoder computation, the final hidden representation supplies the projection that produces Block KV for decoder consumption. The purple K/V blocks follow their own path into the decoder. Start at the full input sequence, follow it to the encoder result, then turn down the projection arrow. This makes the origin of the reusable state explicit. The arrow along the outside of the drawing carries that state toward its consumer while leaving room to examine the separate local-window preparation below.

blocks.title: Decoder: replay the tail on every prefill
blocks.text: The decoder must prepare its layer-local window state. It replays a short prompt suffix on every prefill, whether or not prefix SWA was found. Starting partway through the prompt bounds key visibility by both the sliding window and the replay start, producing approximate SWA state. The faded tokens sit outside this decoder tail replay. Its output is used for decode and is not placed in the prefix cache; the highlighted suffix shows where this preparation work occurs.

blocks.title: Encoder: recover at the prefix boundary
blocks.text: The lab below changes the consumer to the encoder. Block KV determines the prefix hit. Only when prefix SWA is missing does the encoder replay the final block of that matched prefix, alongside the uncached suffix, while preserving existing Block KV. Here the reconstruction interval ends at the matched-prefix boundary. In the main diagram, decoder replay ends at the prompt tail and happens on every prefill. Track those endpoints explicitly when moving between the diagram and the lab.

blocks.title: Which tokens can the query see?
blocks.text: Next, move the query within the replay interval. Each cell represents a token and the highlighted cells show keys visible to that query. At the beginning, the replay start limits the left edge. As the query advances, its local window develops within the available suffix. The upper block rows answer where computation starts; the lower token view answers which positions the current computation can see. Reading them together connects a cache decision to the attention region used during bounded replay.

blocks.title: Why cache state has multiple homes
blocks.text: A [[prefix-cache]] avoids repeated prompt computation, but keeping all state in GPU memory competes with active requests. Global KV can be reused across calls, while local [[swa]] state is bounded by a window. This creates different choices for retaining, transferring and reconstructing state. [[erasure-code|Erasure coding]] adds recoverable redundancy and [[gpudirect-rdma]] provides a supported device-to-device data path. These definitions explain the design vocabulary; they do not themselves establish how a particular storage service is deployed.

blocks.title: Two paths for different state
blocks.text: DeepInfer’s storage service is not open source, so the deployment mechanism here comes from its Q&A. [[block-kv|Block KV]] enters persistent storage. SWA state follows a different path: use an available memory cache, otherwise reconstruct it with bounded replay. A bounded window helps explain that choice, while the actual policy remains a Q&A claim. The transfer diagram distinguishes storage reads, shared host memory and device memory. The term GDR should not collapse those stages into an imaginary path with no intermediate state.

blocks.title: Scenario: resume a conversation later
blocks.text: When a user pauses a conversation, active GPU memory can serve other requests. On return, the entrypoint locates reusable prefix state. Global KV is retrieved from its retained location, while local state is recovered from memory or reconstructed. The public snippet below only shows selecting a window from a local circular state cache; it is not the persistent storage service. It explains why a logical token position differs from a physical buffer slot, without exposing or proving remote erasure-code scheduling.

blocks.title: From directory to device
blocks.text: Before routing, Entrypoint needs the usable prefix length to arrange subsequent work. Data movement follows: KV is fetched into host shared memory and then made available in device memory. Layer-wise movement can overlap forward execution. This separates knowing where state can be found from having it ready for the device to consume. At each arrow, ask which of those conditions has become true. The distinction makes the host-memory stage and the engine-side swap-in stage visible parts of the request journey.

blocks.title: Understand a read
blocks.text: Erasure coding describes how data and redundancy are distributed. The read policy describes the responses required to continue. Sending reads to additional nodes and proceeding once enough responses arrive can reduce dependence on a particular slow response. Read the accompanying parameters in that order: identify the stored fragments, the issued reads, and the completion threshold. Each belongs to a different step of the process. Together they explain a read operation in terms of its layout and its condition for making progress.

blocks.title: Fetch or rebuild SWA
blocks.text: For SWA, the directory records the compute machine holding the state. A later request can use that information to retrieve the still-available state remotely. If it is missing, bounded replay provides a reconstruction route. Think of the branch as the result of a lookup: finding available state leads to retrieval; missing state leads to recovery through computation. Both paths serve the same consumer, which needs a usable local window before continuing the model work that depends on it.

blocks.title: Keep state for later
blocks.text: Availability changes as state is accessed, retained, and reclaimed. The retention figures in the Q&A describe its production capacity and access patterns. For the current request, the relevant question is what can be recovered now. For a future follow-up, it is what this execution leaves available. Connect those two requests across time and the roles of persistence, location tracking, and reconstruction become clear. They cooperate to preserve useful earlier computation while accommodating state that may disappear between visits.

blocks.title: Why request counts are insufficient
blocks.text: Every request may be called a conversation, yet its work can differ greatly. A long prefill has more positions to process; [[chunked-prefill]] breaks that work into schedulable pieces. Decode must consider not just active request count but historical [[kv-cache]] length. Scheduling therefore asks how much work is pending, rather than merely counting records in a queue. Chunking changes the granularity at which the scheduler can intervene, while keeping the prompt’s context dependency intact.

blocks.title: Illustration: equal counts, unequal work
blocks.text: Suppose queue A has prompts of 100 and 100 tokens, while queue B has 1000 and 1000. These are illustrative values. Request counts are equal, but pending positions total 200 and 2000 respectively. Even before accounting for attention context, equal request counts have not equalized prompt work. Real routing also considers cache hits, execution stage and compute budgets. The length ratio in this example must not be presented as a measured latency ratio: hardware and the shape of the operations still matter.

blocks.title: What the public estimator actually shows
blocks.text: The Q&A describes prefill workload buckets and a cost model for chunk selection, while decode uses request counts together with total KV length. The public FLOPs estimator separately computes attention, non-attention and output-projection work. It is a useful example of decomposing a compute budget, not the implementation of the online quadratic latency model or bucket routing. Its return value exposes attention separately while also including it in the total. A caller must not add the separate attention value to that total again.

blocks.title: Pick a load signal
blocks.text: Request count is a natural starting point, but equal counts can hide different context lengths and different work. Expand each branch of the diagram and identify the quantity being observed. Then ask what destination the scheduler chooses and what decision remains for the receiving engine. This turns the branches into a sequence of specific decisions. A request may pass through several of them during its journey, each informed by the part of the workload visible at that stage.

blocks.title: From quota to chunk
blocks.text: Prefill organizes contexts into length tiers and allocates resources according to compute-quota demand. Inside the engine, a further decision determines how much new input fits in the current iteration. The documented time-cost model relates the computed prefix to the additional work; inversion against the remaining budget determines the chunk that can fit. Tiering therefore organizes incoming requests, while the chunk decision sizes concrete work for an available allowance. Follow that progression from the outer branch to the work executed by the device.

blocks.title: Two decode dimensions
blocks.text: Decode considers concurrent request count alongside total KV length. Imagine devices serving similar numbers of requests while one holds much longer contexts. Counting requests would miss that difference in accumulated attention work. Carry both dimensions into the decode branch to understand why the official heuristic treats the placement of short and long requests separately. The branch is easier to read when you track the batch dimension and the context dimension together, rather than compressing them into a single queue count.

blocks.title: Image work
blocks.text: Vision encoding changes the scale again. The same number of images can produce different patch workloads when image sizes differ. Follow the patch-count label back to the encoder work introduced in the system chapter. Each resource pool observes a signal related to its own processing task. The request consequently encounters different allocation decisions as image preparation, input processing, and ongoing generation take place. Keeping the unit of each signal visible makes the reason for those separate branches concrete.

blocks.title: Why output protocol belongs in the inference path
blocks.text: Users see text, tool calls or structured fields, while a model operates on [[token]] IDs. A [[tokenizer]] and [[special-token|special tokens]] preserve boundaries and control information. The output side must reconstruct a usable protocol from incremental results. [[constrained-decoding|Constrained decoding]] restricts candidates while generating, rather than relying only on repairing a completed string afterward. The application boundary is therefore part of the inference path: incorrect encoding or incremental parsing can invalidate otherwise valid model computation.

blocks.title: From grammar state to allowed candidates
blocks.text: An [[automaton]] tracks the structure generated so far, while a [[token-mask]] excludes currently invalid candidates. DeepInfer’s Q&A describes asynchronous grammar compilation and incremental state updates; its public matcher connects grammar matching to the masks used during sampling. A format constraint does not decide whether the content is true or useful. A syntactically valid tool argument can still be inappropriate for a task. Keep the grammar’s acceptance condition separate from application-level validation.

blocks.title: Scenario: a character and a marker span chunks
blocks.text: As an illustration, split the [[utf|UTF-8]] bytes for the character 中 across two network reads. The first part is not a complete character and must be retained until the rest arrives. [[sse|SSE]] event boundaries likewise do not coincide with arbitrary network chunks. If an end marker begins in an old chunk and finishes in a new one, incremental matching must retain progress. [[kmp|KMP]] uses a failure table to fall back to a prefix that can still match, avoiding a fresh scan of all previous output on each chunk.

blocks.title: Keep the input structure
blocks.text: Explicit special tokens inserted by the template retain their identity during encoding. Recording those boundaries lets control markers map directly to their intended IDs while ordinary spans follow text encoding. The spans can be processed separately and their results assembled in the original order. That final ordering carries the conversation structure into the inference engine. Trace a template boundary through the encoding path and it becomes clear how the system preserves the difference between application control structure and ordinary message content.

blocks.title: Constrain sampling
blocks.text: Format constraints first pass through asynchronous compilation to produce a structure usable at runtime. During generation, the matcher advances its state with the output and produces a sampling mask. The arrow joining the sampling stage shows where the constraint participates in selecting the next token. Follow this branch from the requested format to the mask: preparation happens before use, while the runtime state evolves as generation proceeds. This connects the compiler and matcher to a visible decision made during each generation step.

blocks.title: Continue across chunks
blocks.text: A streaming chunk can end inside a character or a delimiter. The parser retains the unfinished portion: UTF-8 buffering handles incomplete characters, incremental matching keeps delimiter progress, and the state machine tracks whether confirmed content belongs to text, reasoning, or tool-related output. When another chunk arrives, parsing continues from that saved state. Mark the boundary between confirmed content and the fragment still awaiting input, then follow how that boundary advances as more of the response becomes available.

Streaming parsers retain incomplete state across chunks.

blocks.title: Expert route: identify each tensor’s role
blocks.text: Several mechanisms meet in a model’s forward path. Recall that a [[residual]] retains an input while adding a transformation, [[sparse-attention]] reads a selected set of positions, and [[sinkhorn]] alternates row and column normalization. These definitions provide vocabulary for following the interfaces; they do not replace evidence for this model’s implementation. This expert chapter traces where data is produced and consumed in the public code, rather than deriving unverified training motivations from inference operations.

blocks.title: Scenario: why shared indices are not enough
blocks.text: Suppose a later layer receives position indices selected by an earlier layer. It still needs the matching KV data and an interpretation of those coordinates. Sharing indices does not automatically mean sharing the cache itself. The public topology object organizes source relationships for KV, indexer K and top-k separately. Its constructor processes configuration, builds mappings and then validates them. Reading these static dependencies first makes the runtime tensors easier to follow: a value can only be reused correctly when its source and consumers agree.

blocks.title: Separate representation from the algorithm
blocks.text: [[ngram-hash|N-gram hashing]] explains addressing a lookup table from consecutive token fragments. [[fp8]] and [[mx]] describe numeric representation and scaling. Lookup, projection, index selection and cache storage answer different questions. When reading a low-precision field, determine whether it applies to weights, activations, the indexer or the main KV. Similar format names are not evidence that all those objects share one representation or scaling granularity. Trace the object as well as the format.

blocks.title: Start with the residual streams
blocks.text: Finally, zoom into the model. This chapter follows interfaces in the pinned code: start with the residual streams entering mHC, then inspect how a side branch contributes to [[hidden-state|hidden state]]s. The main path gives a reading order, while the branches identify modules to open as you trace the relationships.

blocks.title: Follow a side branch back
blocks.text: Take the Engram branch next. An n-gram hash obtains embeddings, which pass through projection and a gate before entering hidden states. Lookup, transformation, and injection are adjacent steps with distinct inputs and outputs. Following them separately turns the branch into a concrete sequence of operations in the implementation.

blocks.title: Trace one mixing operation
blocks.text: The mHC path connects a Sinkhorn call with mixing across residual streams. Identify the incoming streams, then follow where the mixed result goes. This reading method attaches the main-path arrows to inspectable call relationships and gives you an entry point for continuing into the attention and [[moe|MoE]] modules shown in the schematic.

blocks.title: Trace selection and reuse
blocks.text: Follow compressed KV and the indexer as separate inputs to attention. Query scoring produces selected KV indices. Cross-layer topology maintains separate sharing mappings for KV, indexer K, and selected indices; consumers use these relationships to read from earlier source layers. Pick a consumer, find its source layer, then return to the diagram to identify the corresponding reuse path.

blocks.title: Check the representation being used
blocks.text: While tracing data, keep track of the particular weight or cache object you are reading. The official description assigns different format conventions to Main KV, Indexer KV, routed-expert weights, and [[swa|SWA]] KV. Identify the object before reading its format and scaling rule. This connects interface relationships with the representation used by the data moving through them.

reading.scope: This remains a code guide. Paragraphs marked inferred describe calls and data relationships; training motivations and effects are outside what these inference interfaces establish.
takeaways: Read static dependencies before runtime data.
Sharing indices differs from sharing KV.
Separate background, public interfaces and inference.

decodeLab.title: Decode lab: can guessing ahead save time?
decodeLab.intro: Once decoding is underway, another way to save time is to propose candidate tokens and verify them together. Having seen how a batch is scheduled, explore how DSpark chooses the candidates worth checking.
decodeLab.lead: Lower an early confidence slider and watch later candidates lose value too. Then switch to fixed length and compare the choices made from exactly the same proposals.
decodeLab.scope: The sliders and timing curve explain a trade-off. Production allocates a shared budget across requests; official reported results are listed separately in the demo.

background.title: Draft first, then verify
background.text: Ordinary [[autoregressive|autoregressive generation]] selects an output before the next input is known. [[speculative-decoding|Speculative decoding]] proposes a draft first, then checks its known positions in parallel with the target. When weight movement dominates and spare arithmetic capacity remains, verification can approach the cost of a short decode step, but it is not always equally fast. [[acceptance|Acceptance]] determines how much draft survives; verification cost determines the time spent producing it. DSpark then asks how many candidates are worth verifying.

takeaways: Separate drafting from target verification.
Acceptance must be considered alongside verification cost.
The demo curve is illustrative, not a measured speedup.

basics.title: Before you start: from text to computation
basics.intro: Build a few small mental models before following a request into DeepInfer. Hover, click or focus a dotted-underlined term to open its definition.

questions.q: What work does a KV cache save?
questions.a: It saves recomputing old keys and values. Ordinary full attention still reads relevant historical [[kv-cache|KV]].

questions.q: Why allocate separate resources to prompt processing and generation?
questions.a: [[prefill-decode|Prefill and decode]] have different work shapes and typical bottlenecks. Separate resources reduce interference but require state transfer.

questions.q: Can any idle expert replace a busy expert?
questions.a: No. Different logical experts have different weights. An [[expert-replica]] provides another location for the same expert.

basics.kvTitle: Try it: how much KV does context need?
basics.kvScope: Illustrative values · Uncompressed full attention, one sequence, uniform layers; not a DeepInfer estimator. Read volume assumes one complete historical KV read per step, excluding weights, output writes and repeated kernel accesses.
basics.formula: K and V × tokens × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per element
basics.scope: Illustrative playback · Text is prewritten, not an actual tokenizer split or model prediction.

sections.title: What happens inside a conversation
sections.text: Text first passes through a [[tokenizer]] to become [[token]] IDs, then an [[embedding]] turns them into vectors. A forward pass moves those vectors through the model layers; their intermediate representation is called a [[hidden-state]]. The final scores describe candidates for the next position. [[sampling|Sampling]] selects a token and appends it to the sequence, providing input for the next iteration. This [[autoregressive|autoregressive generation]] loop continues until an end marker or length limit. The player below illustrates the loop without running a language model.

sections.title: Why each step need not start again
sections.text: [[attention|Attention]] reads context through [[qkv|queries Q, keys K and values V]]: a query matches historical keys and combines the corresponding values. The [[kv-cache]] stores keys and values of processed positions. The next iteration adds new state while ordinary full attention still reads relevant historical KV. Continuing a conversation therefore need not recompute every old key and value. When compatible state survives between requests, a [[prefix-cache]] can reuse the same beginning. Matching means the same token prefix, not merely similar meaning.

sections.title: Process the prompt, then generate
sections.text: [[prefill-decode|Prefill and decode]] have different work shapes. Prompt positions are already known, so prefill processes many positions together. Ordinary decode handles 1 new position per request per step, with later positions depending on sampling. A sufficiently long prefill tends to occupy the arithmetic units; a small decode batch can instead spend much of its time reading weights and historical KV, making [[bandwidth]] important. This is a tendency, not a universal rule: batch size, attention design and hardware change the bottleneck. In MoE, only relevant activated expert weights are read, rather than every expert in the model.

sections.title: Experts are modules inside the model
sections.text: [[moe|Mixture of experts]] distributes part of the model computation among neural modules. [[expert-routing|Expert routing]] scores a token representation, selects top-k routed experts and combines their outputs; some architectures also use a [[shared-expert]]. Imagine several tokens all choosing one popular expert. Idle experts cannot simply substitute for it because they have different weights. The EPLB chapter explains how physical copies of the same expert help distribute that work. Expert identifiers and the number of connections in this drawing are illustrative.

sections.title: Split the data, or split the model
sections.text: [[dp|Data parallelism]] gives different inputs to matching model replicas. [[tp|Tensor parallelism]] partitions a layer computation, while [[ep|expert parallelism]] distributes experts across devices. EP sends token representations to the selected experts and returns the results using dispatch and combine [[all-to-all]] exchanges. These choices can be combined: the DeepInfer Q&A describes attention DP together with MoE EP. The drawing compares the main DP and EP distinction; its device and expert counts are illustrative.

sections.title: Decide what kind of fast you need
sections.text: [[ttft|TTFT]] asks how soon a reply starts; [[tpot|TPOT]] asks how quickly it continues; [[throughput]] counts total completed work. [[goodput]] also requires meeting latency objectives. High [[gpu-utilization]] only means kernels were active during much of the sampling period; it does not prove all arithmetic units were saturated. To read a performance plot, first check the axis directions and workload, then inspect the [[pareto|Pareto front]]. Points on the front represent tradeoffs. Decide whether responsiveness or capacity matters more before choosing one.
